title: What WJEC Examiners Want
lead: Examiners award marks for knowing the term and for applying it to the item. This page shows the five mistakes that lose marks, the eight habits of full-mark answers, and where the five marks come from.

p: These five mistakes cost marks again and again. Your teacher’s list of examiner comments includes ignoring the item, giving examples without linking them, and repeating material.
list: Defining a different term. A correct definition of the wrong word earns nothing, so read the named term again before you start.
No item link. An answer that never uses the item cannot earn the application marks.
An example with no explanation. An example needs a sentence that says what it shows about the term.
Copying the item. Writing out the item’s words shows that you can read it; the examiner wants to see you use it.
A list with no sentences. A list of key words explains nothing, so write full sentences.

p: These are the top examiner tips from your teacher’s list, with a line on how to use each one.
list: Always use the item. Aim for two explained item links, and explain how the item illustrates the term rather than copying it.
Quote specific words. Pick the exact words from the item that matter and say what they show.
Use sociological terminology. Start with an accurate definition of the named term, using the words the course uses.
Develop explanations. Aim for three developed knowledge points, not three bare statements.
Give clear examples. Choose a relevant example and say how it shows the idea.
Link back to the question. Finish by answering what the question asked.
Distinguish AO1 from AO2. Know which sentences show what you know and which sentences apply it to the item.
Write in PEEL format. In a ten-mark answer, give each paragraph a Point, Evidence, Apply Item, Explain and Link Back.

p: A five-mark question is marked for AO1 knowledge and understanding (3 marks) and AO2 application (2 marks). The marks are not given one for each sentence: examiners reward accurate answers and a good use of the item.

DIET shows where the marks come from. The letters stand for Define the term, Item link, Explain with an example and Theory link. A relevant theory can strengthen an explanation, but a named theory is not an automatic requirement for full marks.
In the five-mark activities on this site, D, E and T are the three AO1 marks, and the two item details in your item link are the two AO2 marks:
list: D, Define the term (AO1): an accurate definition of the term in the question.
I, Item link (AO2): the place where you apply the term to the item, using specific words from it. Aim for two explained item links; you do not need to quote the item twice.
E, Explain with an example (AO1): a relevant example, with a sentence that explains it.
T, Theory link (AO1): a brief, relevant link to a perspective, such as Functionalists or Feminists.
